title: Piccolo-27B Tops Decision Index After Self-Improvement Loop
summary: Alaya Lab's Piccolo-27B scores 75.59 on Decision Index Vision, ranking first overall. The 0.8B-27B family used recursive self-improvement across 600
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Alaya Lab released Piccolo, a 0.8B to 27B parameter multimodal decision model family that ranks first on Decision Index Vision.
- Piccolo-27B scored 75.59 overall, with smaller 9B and 4B variants topping their size tiers through recursive self-improvement training.
- Training spanned roughly 600 experimental runs and 6,300 accelerator-hours, with weights and orchestration tools open-sourced today.


Alaya Lab released Piccolo, a family of multimodal decision models ranging from 0.8B to 27B parameters, on November 19, 2026. The flagship Piccolo-27B scores 75.59 on the[Decision Index Vision](https://emergent.sh/news/decision-index-v2-drex-max-fastino-glide-tie) Full leaderboard, claiming the top overall ranking. Smaller siblings Piccolo-9B and Piccolo-4B scored 68.35 and 67.46 respectively, each placing first in their size categories on the Private benchmark. Training employed a recursive self-improvement loop that turned roughly 600 experimental runs into cumulative scientific discovery rather than brute-force hyperparameter search.


## Release Date and Availability


Officially released on November 19, 2026, Piccolo weights are available alongside the Data-Juicer data stack and AgentScope orchestration ecosystem. The release coincides with another multimodal launch tracked the same day, inside a 90-day window that has carried 122 multimodal stories through industry feeds. All model sizes from 0.8B to 27B parameters are open-sourced, enabling researchers to replicate the agentic training loop on custom datasets.


## Benchmark Performance and Rankings


Piccolo-27B posted a 75.59 full score and 70.97 private score on Decision Index Vision, securing the number-one position overall. The 9B variant achieved 68.35 and the 4B variant scored 67.46, both leading their respective size tiers. According to the paper, targeted data curation at the 4B and 9B scales rivals untargeted 27B baselines on specialized workflows, challenging conventional assumptions that larger always means better for domain-specific tasks.


## Recursive Self-Improvement Training


The core innovation is a training loop in which research agents propose data slices, execute experiments, and refine proposals based on weight-space trajectories and training dynamics. The authors bind fine-grained semantic slices, training curves, and model checkpoints into a persistent research memory, transforming what would be random hyperparameter search into directed exploration. Across the 0.8B to 27B family, this process consumed approximately 6,300 PPU-ZW810E accelerator-hours over roughly 600 experimental runs.


## Counterintuitive Training Findings


Three results challenge standard recipes. First, earlier backbone architectures can outperform newer generations on visual tasks when recipe and data remain constant. Second, dynamic data curation proves more compute-efficient than prolonged static training, with continuous loss reduction sometimes decoupling from, or even degrading, discrete decision accuracy. Third, the 4B and 9B models match or exceed 27B baselines on specialized workflows through targeted curation, suggesting that model scale is not the only lever for performance gains.


- Piccolo-27B ranks first overall on Decision Index Vision with a 75.59 full score.
- Training spanned roughly 600 experiments and 6,300 accelerator-hours using recursive agent loops.
- Smaller 4B and 9B variants top their size tiers, challenging the assumption that larger models always win.
- Open-source release includes weights, Data-Juicer stack, and AgentScope orchestration tools.


## What This Means


Piccolo demonstrates that agentic data engineering and recursive self-improvement can compete with, and in some cases surpass, brute-force scaling on decision benchmarks. By encoding experimental history into agent memory, Alaya Lab turns model training into a cumulative research process rather than isolated runs. The open-source release of weights and orchestration infrastructure lowers the barrier for teams pursuing similar agentic training loops, potentially accelerating research into multimodal decision systems across academia and industry.
